title: Public Health
description: Ten clear, reflective texts about public health: clean water in the nineteenth-century city, John Snow and the Broad Street pump, tracking a flu season, handwashing in hospitals, a school nurse's year, the history of the seat belt, sleep, a community health worker on the prairie, oyster beds and clean water, and walking soccer for older adults.

lessons.title: How Clean Water Changed the City
lessons.summary: A short history of how sewers, pipes and filters made nineteenth-century cities healthier, and what water recycling means today.
lessons.text:
If you could take a stroll through a large city of the early nineteenth century, your nose would notice the problem before your eyes did. In London, New York or Paris, most families had no running water and no toilet of their own. Waste was collected in pits behind the houses, and in poorer streets it was piled in mounds that waited, sometimes for weeks, for someone to cart them away.

Water came from public pumps, wells and rivers, and the same rivers often carried the city's waste. For the poor, getting water was a daily hardship. A girl might carry heavy buckets up four flights of stairs before breakfast, and the water she carried was not always clean. Many of the poorest families lived in cellars below the street, damp rooms with little light that visitors compared to a dungeon. When the river rose, dirty water flowed into these dungeon homes.

Diseases carried by water, such as cholera and typhoid, could kill thousands of people in a single bad year. Yet many doctors still believed that such diseases came from bad air.

Change came slowly, and it came through engineering. In the unusually hot summer of 1858, the smell from the river in London became so strong that members of Parliament could hardly work. The city decided to build a great system of sewers. The engineer Joseph Bazalgette designed brick tunnels that carried the waste away from the homes. He made them much larger than anyone thought necessary, so that they could withstand the growth of the city for a century. They have withstood far more than that: many of his tunnels are still in use today.

Other cities followed. They brought clean water from lakes and hills through long pipes and began to filter it. Year by year, the old public pumps were dismantled and the pits behind the houses were filled in. It took decades to dismantle the old system, but the change was noticeable almost at once. There was a noticeable fall in deaths, and children in particular began to live longer. Some historians argue that clean water did more for health in that century than any medicine.

Clean water also changed daily life in quieter ways. When water came from a tap, girls no longer spent hours carrying buckets, and more of them stayed in school. A stroll by the river became a pleasure instead of a hardship.

Today the work goes on out of sight. Modern plants clean used water so well that some cities now practice water recycling. The cleaned water is used for parks and factories, and in a few unusually dry places it is cleaned again until it is safe to drink. Water recycling may sound strange, but the idea behind it is old: a city, like a body, stays healthy only when what goes out does not come back in.

Questions:
Why was getting water a hardship for poor families?
They had to carry heavy buckets from pumps, wells and rivers, and the water was not always clean.
How was waste handled in poorer streets in the nineteenth century?
It was piled in mounds that waited, sometimes for weeks, for someone to cart them away.
Why did Joseph Bazalgette make his tunnels so large?
He wanted them to withstand the growth of the city for a century.
What is water recycling?
It is cleaning used water so that it can be used again, for parks, for factories or even for drinking.

lessons.title: John Snow and the Broad Street Pump
lessons.summary: In 1854 a London doctor maps a cholera outbreak, traces it to one water pump and slowly changes medical opinion.
lessons.text:
In the summer of 1854, a sudden outbreak of cholera struck Soho, a crowded district in the center of London. Within ten days, more than 500 people who lived within a few streets of each other had died. Most doctors could not comprehend why the disease had chosen this small area. The common view was that cholera spread through bad air.

One doctor was stubborn enough to doubt this. John Snow was a quiet, careful man who had studied cholera for years. He had noticed that the disease attacked the gut, not the lungs, and he reasoned that people must swallow something, most likely dirty water, rather than breathe it in. His view was a dissent from the medical opinion of the time, and few colleagues took it seriously.

When the outbreak began, Snow went from door to door, asking families where they got their water. He marked each death on a street map with a small black bar. The pattern was striking: the bars gathered around a public water pump on Broad Street. In 1854, photographic cameras were still rare and slow, and there is no photographic record of those streets in the outbreak. What survives instead is Snow's map, which made an invisible pattern visible.

His whole case would hinge on that pattern, so he paid special attention to the exceptions. A workhouse near the pump, home to hundreds of poor people, had very few deaths; it had its own well. The men at a brewing company on the same street were almost all spared as well. The brewing of beer involves boiling the water, and the workers were given beer to drink, so they hardly touched the pump. Every exception seemed to hinge on the same question: did these people drink from Broad Street or not?

Snow presented his evidence to the local officials, and on September 8 they agreed to remove the handle of the pump. The outbreak was already fading by then, so historians still debate how much this single act achieved. What is not debated is the method, which is now seen as one of the founding works of public health.

It took many years to overturn the theory of bad air. A local priest, Henry Whitehead, at first set out to prove Snow wrong. He was as stubborn as Snow, but as he interviewed the families again, he began to comprehend that Snow was right. Snow died in 1858, before his dissent became the accepted view. Some people feel that the medical world betrayed him by ignoring his work for so long. Others reply that he was not so much betrayed as ahead of his time: science often needs years to overturn an old idea, even when the evidence is good.

Today, visitors to Broadwick Street, as Broad Street is now called, can see a replica of the famous pump, without a handle. The replica was first unveiled in 1992, and after building work on the street it was unveiled again in 2018.

Questions:
What did most doctors believe about cholera in 1854?
They believed that it spread through bad air.
How did Snow find the pattern of the outbreak?
He asked families where they got their water and marked each death on a street map.
Why were the workers at the brewing company spared?
They were given beer to drink, so they hardly touched the pump water.
What can visitors see on Broadwick Street today?
They can see a replica of the famous pump, without a handle.

lessons.title: How a Flu Season Is Tracked
lessons.summary: A short report on the signals health agencies combine each week to follow the flu, from doctors' visits to home tests.
lessons.text:
Every autumn, public health agencies begin a quiet task: they watch the flu. In one sense, flu seasons are predictable. In the northern half of the world, they almost always arrive between October and March. In other ways, they are not predictable at all. No one knows in advance how large a season will be or when it will peak. Tracking the flu means turning thousands of small signals into one clear picture, week by week.

In the United States, the flagship of this work is a weekly report from the national health agency, the CDC. Like the flagship of a fleet, the ship that carries the admiral, it leads and gathers the rest. It brings together several kinds of data, each of which tells only part of the story.

The first kind comes from doctors. Across the country, about 3,000 clinics and doctors' offices report each week what share of their patients came in with a fever and a cough or sore throat. These visits are not all flu, but when their share rises, flu is usually the reason. Laboratories report which strains they find, and hospitals report how many patients they admit with flu.

Some reports are voluntary, but others are statutory, which means that a law requires them. In the United States, every death of a child from flu must be reported. A statutory duty of this kind ensures that the most serious cases are never missed, even in a quiet year.

Deaths are also tracked through pneumonia. In some patients, especially the very old and the very young, flu spreads deep into the lungs and causes pneumonia. The lungs contain millions of tiny air sacs, where oxygen passes into the blood, and in pneumonia these sacs fill with fluid, which makes breathing hard. Because flu is often not named on a death certificate, agencies count deaths from pneumonia and flu together as one signal.

New tools have been added in recent years. Many people now test themselves at home with a lateral flow test, a small plastic strip that shows a line within minutes. A lateral flow test is less accurate than a laboratory test, and most home results are never reported, but even the sale of these tests is a clue. Another enhancement is the testing of used water from city sewers, which can show a rise in the virus before people feel sick enough to see a doctor. Each enhancement makes the picture a little sharper.

What experts watch most closely is not the number of cases but their acceleration: how fast the weekly rise is speeding up. A slow rise gives hospitals time to prepare, while a sudden acceleration warns them to make room for more patients.

The data are not equally good everywhere. Some states have stellar reporting systems, with fast and complete numbers; in others, the numbers arrive late. Even with stellar data, a flu forecast is closer to a weather report than to a promise: useful, careful and sometimes wrong.

Questions:
In what sense are flu seasons predictable?
In the northern half of the world, they almost always arrive between October and March.
What happens in the lungs in pneumonia?
The tiny air sacs fill with fluid, which makes breathing hard.
What is a lateral flow test?
It is a small plastic strip that people use at home, which shows a line within minutes.
Why do experts watch the acceleration of cases?
A sudden acceleration warns hospitals to make room for more patients.

lessons.title: Clean Hands in the Hospital
lessons.summary: How a doctor in Vienna showed that handwashing saves lives, why he lost his post, and how hospitals keep hands clean today.
lessons.text:
In 1846, a young Hungarian doctor named Ignaz Semmelweis began work in the maternity department of the great public hospital in Vienna. The department had two clinics, and the difference between them troubled him. In the first clinic, where medical students were trained, about one mother in ten died of a fever soon after giving birth. In the second, where midwives were trained, the rate was far lower.

Semmelweis compared the two clinics closely, and the answer he reached was simple. The students often came to the mothers straight from the room where they studied the bodies of patients who had died, and they did not clean their hands in between. In 1847, he ordered everyone in his clinic to wash their hands in a chlorine solution before examining a patient. Within months, deaths in the first clinic fell to the level of the second.

You might expect that he was praised. Instead, many senior doctors refused to conform to his rule, partly because it suggested that doctors themselves were carrying disease. Semmelweis did not help his own cause: he was slow to publish his results and quick to insult his critics. In 1849, his post was not renewed, and the termination of his contract forced him to leave Vienna. Some later writers described his dismissal as persecution. Historians today see less persecution than a mixture of hospital politics, a difficult personality and a theory that came before germs were understood.

Today, the rule Semmelweis fought for is everywhere. Hospital corridors have stainless steel sinks and dispensers of alcohol gel at every door. Stainless steel is chosen because it is smooth and easy to clean. In many hospitals, a small microcontroller inside each dispenser counts how often it is used and sends the numbers to a computer. The microcontroller cannot tell who is washing, but it shows which wards are falling behind.

Many hospitals also ask staff to keep their arms bare below the elbow. Watches, rings and long sleeves are not allowed, and the reason is the cuff: a shirt cuff touches one patient after another and is rarely washed during the day.

Studies show that staff conform best when they know the rules are checked and least when they are tired or busy. For this reason, many hospitals use trained observers and give each ward regular feedback. Repeated failures can lead to a warning, and in rare cases even to the termination of a contract.

Constant washing has a cost too. Gel and soap dry the skin, and sore, cracked hands are a common occupational problem among nurses. Occupational health teams in hospitals therefore supply creams to soften the skin, and many nurses use them at the end of each shift, since healthy skin is easier to keep clean. It is a small detail, but Semmelweis would have understood it: a rule works only if people can follow it every day.

Questions:
What rule did Semmelweis make in 1847?
He ordered everyone in his clinic to wash their hands in a chlorine solution before examining a patient.
How do historians today see the dismissal of Semmelweis?
They see less persecution than a mixture of hospital politics, a difficult personality and an early theory.
What does the microcontroller inside a dispenser do?
It counts how often the dispenser is used and sends the numbers to a computer.
Why do nurses use cream to soften their hands?
Constant washing dries the skin, and healthy skin is easier to keep clean.

lessons.title: A School Nurse's Year
lessons.summary: A high school nurse describes one school year, from a sophomore's bruise in September to the thank-you notes in June.
lessons.text:
I have been the nurse at a public high school for eleven years, and no two years are the same. Still, every school year has a shape, and this is the shape of the last one.

In September, my office is busiest. The new freshmen get lost, forget their lunches and arrive with headaches that are really nerves. On the second day, a sophomore named Danny came in with a large bruise on his arm from soccer practice. A year earlier he had been a nervous freshman; as a sophomore, he was mostly worried that the bruise would keep him off the team. I gave him ice, wrote a note for his coach and told him that a bruise changes color from blue to green to yellow as it heals, which he found fascinating.

In November, the first colds arrive, followed by the flu. A math teacher who still writes on a board with chalk asked me why her students coughed more in her room than in others. The chalk dust, it turned out, bothered a girl with asthma, and the school gave the teacher a new board that uses markers. She missed her chalk, but the coughing stopped.

In January, the school librarian and I make posters about sleep and handwashing for the halls. The librarian has an eye for design, and I supply the facts. This year we also set up a table of books about health, and the librarian told me that the books about sleep were borrowed most.

Spring is the season of art projects and small accidents. In March, a boy came in with glitter in his eye after an art class. I washed the eye gently with clean water until the glitter was gone, and he went back to class with a red eye and a good story. In April, before the spring dance, I noticed several girls sharing one lipstick in the hall. I gave a short, friendly talk on why lipstick, like a toothbrush, is best kept to yourself, since cold sores pass easily from person to person. The next day, one of the girls showed me her own new lipstick.

The most amusing visit of the year came in May. A senior arrived holding his trousers together with both hands. He had torn them on a fence and wanted me to sew them before his class photo. Luckily, my kit contains a needle and thread. The trousers held for the photo, and he called it the most amusing emergency of his life.

On the last day of school, a few students leave notes on my door. I admit that I am a sucker for those notes. I keep them all in a box in my desk. A nurse who is a sucker for thank-you notes, I have learned, never runs out of reasons to come back in September.

Questions:
Why did Danny come to the nurse's office?
He had a large bruise on his arm from soccer practice.
Why did the students cough more in the math teacher's room?
The chalk dust bothered a girl with asthma.
Why did the nurse give a talk about lipstick?
Several girls were sharing one lipstick, and cold sores pass easily from person to person.
What is the nurse a sucker for?
She is a sucker for the thank-you notes that students leave on her door.

lessons.title: A Short History of the Seat Belt
lessons.summary: How the seat belt went from a rare extra to a normal part of driving, thanks to doctors, an engineer and years of campaigns.
lessons.text:
Today, most drivers put on a seat belt without a thought. Seventy years ago, few cars even had one.

In the early years of the car, a crash was treated as bad luck, or as the fault of a bad driver. Cars were built to look good, not to protect the people inside. As cars grew faster and roads more crowded, the number of deaths on the road rose to horrific levels. Doctors in emergency rooms saw serious head injuries every weekend, and some patients fell into a coma. Some of them began to argue that the car itself was part of the problem.

At first, belts were an extra. In 1956, one car company in the United States offered lap belts as an option, a deluxe extra like a radio or special seat covers. Few buyers paid for the deluxe package. Some Grand Prix drivers of the time refused to wear belts, believing that it was safer to be thrown clear of a crash. It took years before Grand Prix racing accepted the full harness.

The great step came from Sweden. The president of Volvo, who was at the helm of the company from 1956, had made safety a priority, and in 1958 the company hired an engineer named Nils Bohlin, who had designed escape seats for fighter pilots. Bohlin was given the helm of the project and a simple task: design a belt that people would actually wear. His answer, presented in 1959, was the three-point belt, with one strap across the hips and another across the chest, joined at a single buckle beside the seat. It held the body tightly across its strongest bones. Volvo then let other companies use the design for free.

But a belt helps only if it is worn. The first state law in the United States that required adults to wear belts came in 1984, in New York. Laws alone were not enough; they needed reinforcement. Police checks, school programs and advertising campaigns all played a part, and bumper stickers asked drivers to buckle up. This reinforcement worked slowly but surely, and today about nine in ten drivers in the United States wear a belt. Cars changed too: bumpers were made to absorb small knocks, and frames were designed to fold at the front while protecting the passengers.

No belt can prevent a crash. A driver who tries to overtake a truck on a narrow road, or who overtakes on a hill without seeing what is coming, still takes a serious risk. A modern car with a turbo engine can reach high speeds in seconds. Yet if something goes wrong, the turbo car of today protects its passengers far better than the slow cars of seventy years ago, partly because the belt holds them tightly in place. A crash that might once have ended in a coma now often ends with nothing worse than a bruise. The numbers from the early years were horrific; the numbers today are a quiet success.

Questions:
How were seat belts sold in 1956?
They were sold as a deluxe extra, like a radio or special seat covers.
Why did some Grand Prix drivers refuse to wear belts?
They believed it was safer to be thrown clear of a crash.
What did Nils Bohlin design in 1959?
He designed the three-point belt, with one strap across the hips and another across the chest.
Why did laws need reinforcement?
Many people still did not wear belts, so police checks, school programs and campaigns were needed too.

lessons.title: The Public Health Case for Sleep
lessons.summary: A column on why sleep matters for the brain, for safety on the roads and for night workers, and what makes it hard to get enough.
lessons.text:
Ask people what they do for their health, and they will tell you about food and exercise. Few will mention sleep, yet sleep may be the most neglected habit in public health. Surveys in the United States suggest that about a third of adults regularly sleep less than seven hours a night, the minimum that most experts recommend.

While we sleep, the brain is far from idle. Its neural networks replay and sort the day's experiences, which helps to fix memories. Scientists have also found that during deep sleep, fluid moves through the brain more freely and helps to wash away the waste left by neural activity. A tired brain is, quite literally, a brain that has not finished cleaning up.

The effects reach far beyond the individual. Tired drivers cause a large share of road accidents, because sleep can ambush a tired driver: the eyes close for a few seconds, without warning, at seventy miles an hour. Such an ambush is most likely in the early hours of the morning and on long, straight roads.

Some people have little choice about sleeping badly. Think of a waiter who works the late shift in a nightclub. The nightclub closes at three, the waiter helps to clean up and gets home at four, and he tries to sleep while the city is loud and bright. Night workers like him, along with nurses, drivers and factory staff, sleep less on average and have higher rates of several health problems. Public health, in other words, is not only about personal choices. It is also about how work is arranged.

For the rest of us, the enemies of sleep are more ordinary. Work is greedy, and so are our phones: both will take as many hours as we give them. A greedy phone in the bedroom, glowing and buzzing, is a poor companion at midnight. There is also a cultural problem. Many people admire the persona of the heroic worker who needs only four hours a night. That persona looks impressive in films, but in real life it usually belongs to someone who is tired and slower than they think.

What would a healthier approach look like? It need not be classy or expensive. Some classy hotels now offer "sleep menus" with a choice of pillows, but the basics that experts describe are free: regular hours for sleep, a dark and cool room, and some quiet time without screens before bed. Communities can help too, by reducing noise at night and by letting high schools start a little later, since the body clocks of teenagers run late.

The reward is real. Anyone who has slept well after a long, hard week knows the heavenly feeling of waking up rested, a few minutes before the alarm. That heavenly feeling is not a luxury. It is a sign that the body has done one of its most important jobs.

Questions:
What does the brain do while we sleep?
Its neural networks sort the day's experiences, and fluid helps to wash away waste.
How can sleep ambush a tired driver?
The driver's eyes close for a few seconds, without warning, at high speed.
What persona do many people admire?
They admire the persona of the heroic worker who needs only four hours a night.
What is the heavenly feeling the writer describes?
It is the feeling of waking up rested, a few minutes before the alarm.

lessons.title: A Health Worker on the Prairie
lessons.summary: A profile of a community health worker who drives between small prairie towns, helping families get the care they need.
lessons.text:
In the small towns of the northern prairie, the nearest hospital can be an hour's drive away, and many people see a doctor only when something is already wrong. Rosa Delgado's job is to close that gap. She is a community health worker: not a nurse or a doctor, but a trained member of the community who visits people at home, helps them understand their care and connects them with the services they need.

Rosa grew up on the prairie. Her parents came from Mexico to work on a hog farm, and she spent her childhood among long barns, the smell of hogs and a sky that seemed to have no end. She and her husband were wed in the small church where she still plays the trumpet every Sunday.

Her working day begins early. She drives up to 200 miles, from one farm to the next, with a box of forms, a blood pressure monitor and a bottle of coffee. One morning she might help an older man understand his new medicines. In the afternoon, she might help a couple who were wed only last year to sign up for health insurance before their first baby arrives. Often a visit ends at the kitchen table, where she is invited to stay for supper. She rarely says no to supper, because the most honest conversations happen over food.

Rosa has learned to tread carefully. People on the prairie are proud and private, and a stranger who asks too many questions is not welcome. She treads gently, listens more than she talks and lets each family decide what they want to discuss. "Trust comes first," she says. "Without trust, the forms are just paper."

Some of her clients are smokers who want to quit. Rosa does not lecture them. She asks each smoker why he or she wants to stop, and she builds a plan around that reason: a grandchild, the cost, or the wish to climb stairs without stopping. When a smoker is ready, she connects them with a free program and calls every week to see how it is going.

Studies of community health workers suggest that people who receive such visits keep more of their appointments and make fewer emergency trips to hospitals. For Rosa, the evidence is more personal. In her car, she keeps a card with a line from a psalm that her mother loved, about lifting one's eyes to the hills. There are no hills on the prairie, she says with a smile, so she lifts her eyes to the sky instead. On Sunday evenings, she practices the trumpet, which clears her head after a week of other people's worries, and she reads the psalm again before a new week begins.

Questions:
What does a community health worker do?
She visits people at home, helps them understand their care and connects them with the services they need.
Where did Rosa grow up?
She grew up on the prairie, on a hog farm where her parents worked.
Why does Rosa rarely say no to supper?
The most honest conversations happen over food.
Why does Rosa tread carefully?
People on the prairie are proud and private, and a stranger who asks too many questions is not welcome.
How does Rosa help a smoker who wants to quit?
She asks why the smoker wants to stop and builds a plan around that reason.

lessons.title: Why Oyster Beds Close After Rain
lessons.summary: An oyster farmer explains why the state tests his waters and closes his beds after storms.
lessons.text:
On a gray morning in Washington State, Tom Becker moors his small boat at a wooden dock and checks his phone before he does anything else. He is not reading the news. He is checking whether the state has closed his oyster beds.

Oysters feed by filtering water. A single adult oyster can pump about 50 gallons of water through its body in a day, eating tiny plants and taking in whatever else the water carries. That makes oysters good for a bay: they clean the water and remove nitrogen, a nutrient that in large amounts feeds harmful blooms of algae. But it also means that when the water is dirty, the oyster is dirty too. Because many people eat oysters raw, the waters where they grow are among the most closely watched in the country. Health officials test the water and the oysters for bacteria and other dangers, and they close a bed whenever the results are bad.

The biggest danger comes from rain. After a gale, or a storm that seems to drop enough rain to float an ark, water rushes off the land into the bay. It carries soil, waste from farm animals and sometimes the overflow from old septic tanks. Up the river from Tom's farm, the hills are covered in vineyards, and the rain that runs off a vineyard can carry fertilizer, which adds even more nitrogen to the water. After heavy rain, the state usually closes the beds for several days, until tests show that the water is clean again. Tom says that in a wet winter, with one gale after another, he sometimes feels he should be building an ark instead of farming oysters.

The geology of the bay matters too. Tom's beds lie on firm gravel left by glaciers thousands of years ago, and gravel stays cleaner than the soft mud of some other bays. Tom studied geology in college, and he can explain the geology of every beach in the bay.

Closures cost him money, but Tom does not complain about them. "One bad oyster can make a person very sick," he says, "and then people stop trusting all of us." He works with other people in the valley to protect the water. Several farmers have planted trees along their streams, and the owner of the largest vineyard has changed how and when he uses fertilizer.

In town, Tom buys his rope and paint from the ship chandler, an old shop that sells supplies to boat owners. The chandler's window still holds a net hung with old cork floats from the days before plastic, when fishermen used cork to keep their nets on the surface. By late afternoon, Tom is back at the dock, where he moors the boat for the night, and the news on his phone is good: the beds are open again.

Questions:
Why does Tom check his phone before he does anything else?
He is checking whether the state has closed his oyster beds.
How do oysters help a bay?
They clean the water and remove nitrogen.
Why does the state close the beds after heavy rain?
Rain carries soil, animal waste and fertilizer into the bay, so the water may be dirty.
Why does the geology of the bay matter?
Tom's beds lie on firm gravel, which stays cleaner than soft mud.
What does the ship chandler sell?
The chandler sells rope, paint and other supplies to boat owners.

lessons.title: Walking Soccer
lessons.summary: Older adults in a small city play a slow version of soccer and discover how much moving together does for their health.
lessons.text:
Every Tuesday morning, a group of men and women aged between 60 and 85 meet at a park in Ohio to play soccer. There is one rule that surprises visitors: nobody is allowed to run. In walking soccer, one foot must always be on the ground, and a player who breaks into a run gives the ball to the other team.

The game began in England as a way to keep older people active, and it has spread to many countries. Its appeal is easy to understand. Players walk upright, so the game is gentle on knees and hips, and there is little risk of a fall, yet it still raises the heart rate and keeps the mind busy.

Frank Russo, 72, played professionally for two seasons in his twenties, for a small team that few people remember. He was a winger, the player who races up the side of the field and sends the ball into the middle. "As a winger, speed was everything," he says. "Now I have to think instead of run." He had not played for forty years when his doctor told him to move more. Frank and his neighbor Walt made a pact: neither of them would miss a Tuesday without a good reason. They have kept the pact for three years.

The top scorer this season is Helen Kowalski, who is 78 and never played soccer before she retired. For years she played squash, until her knees told her to stop. Squash, she says, taught her to watch the ball and the angles, and walking soccer gave her back the pleasure of a game. Being the top scorer pleases her, but she plays for the company more than for the goals.

The benefits of moving are well known. One of the clearest examples comes from space. Astronauts who spend months on a spacecraft lose bone and muscle quickly, because their bodies no longer work against gravity. Long days on a sofa are a slow version of life on a spacecraft. Regular movement, even at a walking pace, helps to protect muscles, bones, balance and the heart.

Yet the players talk most about something else. Many older people spend long days alone, and isolation can harm health as much as sitting still does. On Tuesday mornings, nobody is alone. After the game, the group drinks coffee in a nearby café and talks about grandchildren, gardens and old matches. Frank calls the effect phenomenal. "I came for my knees," he says, "and I stayed for the people." Helen agrees. For her, the change in her mood has been phenomenal, and she has not missed a Tuesday since she joined.

When the coffee is finished, the players walk slowly to their cars, standing upright, still arguing about a goal that may or may not have counted. Next Tuesday, they will be back.

Questions:
What is the main rule of walking soccer?
Nobody is allowed to run, and one foot must always be on the ground.
What position did Frank play when he played professionally?
He was a winger, the player who races up the side of the field.
What pact did Frank and Walt make?
They agreed that neither of them would miss a Tuesday without a good reason.
What sport did Helen play before walking soccer?
She played squash until her knees told her to stop.
Why do astronauts on a spacecraft lose bone and muscle?
Their bodies no longer work against gravity.
